Surgical Breast Enlargement

Breast Lift Risks: What to Know Before You Decide

A lift is a major operation on the breast’s blood supply and skin. Understanding the risks supports informed consent.

Home/Surgical Breast Enlargement/Breast lift/Breast Lift Risks: What to Know Before You Decide

A lift is a major operation on the breast’s blood supply and skin. Understanding the risks supports informed consent and realistic expectations.

General risks

  • Bleeding and haematoma
  • Infection
  • Reactions to anaesthesia
  • Blood clots
  • Delayed wound healing, especially at scar junctions

Risks specific to a lift

  • Scarring: visible, widened or thickened scars
  • Nipple and areola blood supply: because the nipple is moved, its blood supply can be compromised. Serious loss is uncommon, but it can occur, particularly in smokers or with large lifts
  • Sensation changes: reduced, lost or heightened nipple and breast sensation
  • Asymmetry: differences in shape, size or nipple position
  • Contour irregularities or fat necrosis lumps
  • Breastfeeding effects: many people can still breastfeed, but it is not guaranteed
  • Recurrent sagging: gravity and ageing continue to act
  • Need for revision

Factors that raise risk

  • Smoking
  • Large breasts or extensive lifts
  • Significant weight change
  • Conditions affecting healing, such as poorly controlled diabetes

Risk is personal, not a checklist score

A complication can be uncommon overall but still matter greatly to a particular person. Ask which risks are most relevant to your anatomy, medicines, smoking or nicotine use and planned operation, how they would be recognised, and what treatment or revision could involve.

Seroma and delayed healing

Fluid can collect under the skin (seroma), and small areas of the wound may heal slowly, especially where incisions meet. These problems are usually manageable with drainage, dressings or antibiotics, but they can prolong recovery and affect scarring.

Anaesthesia and general health

Anaesthetic risk depends on your health, medicines and history. A preoperative assessment may identify conditions that need treatment before surgery. Report sleep apnoea, bleeding disorders, previous clots and all supplements.

What to tell your surgeon

Be explicit about smoking, nicotine products, weight change and any plan for pregnancy. These factors affect tissue healing and the timing of surgery.

Combining with implants

Combining a lift with an implant increases complexity. Some surgeons stage the two operations for safety.

Reducing risk

  • Stop smoking well before surgery
  • Reach a stable weight
  • Follow aftercare instructions
  • Choose a surgeon who performs lifts regularly

Questions to ask

  • Which risks are most relevant for me?
  • How do you protect the nipple’s blood supply?
  • What is your approach if healing is delayed?

Key takeaway

The risks are manageable when you are well prepared, but they are real. Ask how your surgeon prevents, recognises and treats them.
